draft.title: Linking language in comparison
card: Linking language shows a reader how two texts relate. It signals the direction of the comparison from one sentence to the next.
words such as similarly, likewise and both show that two texts share an idea or method. They tell the reader to expect a match.
words such as in contrast, whereas and however show that the texts part ways. Phrases such as by reshaping show how a later text changes an idea from an earlier one.
A linking word only points the way. The sentence after it must explain how and why the texts connect, using evidence from both. Without that, the word does no work.
draft.remember: A linking word signals the comparison. The explanation after it does the comparing.

a.q: What must a student do after using a linking word such as whereas in a comparative essay?
opts: Explain how the two texts differ and why it matters
Repeat the word in the next sentence for emphasis
Move on to a new idea in the same text
Add a second linking word to strengthen the link
a.why: A linking word signals a difference, but the reader still needs to know what the difference is and why it matters. Adding more linking words is tempting, but it only adds signals and gives no explanation.
a.clue: The word points the way. What must follow it?

b.q: Which sentence uses linking language the way a strong comparative essay should?
opts: Whereas Text A mourns the past, Text B treats it as a comfort
In contrast, the two texts differ and treat memory in their own ways
Similarly, both texts are about memory, and they also differ a lot
Likewise, Text A and Text B each explore memory in some way
b.why: The first sentence uses whereas and then states exactly how the two views of the past differ. The second is the tempting wrong answer: it has a linking phrase, but nothing after it says how the texts differ.
b.clue: Which sentence says what the difference actually is?
